group.passage: On one autumn night each year, tiny flames appear on windowsills, doorsteps and rooftops all over India. They come from diyas, small clay lamps that burn oil, and they give the festival its name: Diwali, or Deepavali, comes from Sanskrit words meaning a row of lights. Because the festival follows the moon rather than the Western calendar, its main night, which is the night of a new moon, falls on a different date each year, usually in October or November. The custom is old. In the 11th century, the Persian scholar Al Biruni described Hindus lighting oil lamps on temples and rooftops on the night of a new moon. The meaning of the lamps differs from place to place. In northern India they recall Prince Rama, who came home to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile and was welcomed with lamps. Many families also clean their homes to welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth, while Sikhs and Jains remember events from their own histories. Behind all these stories lies one idea: light defeating darkness. The celebration lasts five days. Families shop, decorate their floors with rangoli patterns made of colored powder or flower petals, and light rows of lamps. On the fourth day, relatives and friends visit one another with gifts and boxes of sweets such as gulab jamun and jalebi. For India’s potters, the festival matters in another way. Potters in one Mumbai neighborhood say they make about half of their yearly sales in the month before Diwali. In 2016, a handmade clay lamp sold for about 50 US cents, while a cheaper plastic one from abroad cost about a quarter, yet sellers said that people who want the real thing keep coming back to them. The festival keeps growing. On 19 October 2025, Ayodhya lit 2,617,215 clay lamps along its river, setting a world record. Fireworks are popular too, though their smoke adds to air pollution, and New Delhi has banned them in recent years. In December 2025, Diwali was added to UNESCO’s list of the world’s living cultural traditions, a festival now shared by more than a billion people.

translation_zh.text:
每年秋天的某個夜晚，印度各地的窗台、門階和屋頂上都會出現小小的火光。這些火光來自 diya——一種燒油的小陶燈，也讓這個節日有了名字：Diwali（又稱 Deepavali）來自梵文，意思是「一排燈」。因為這個節日跟著月亮走，而不是依照西方的曆法，所以它主要的那一夜——新月之夜——每年日期都不同，通常在十月或十一月。

這個習俗由來已久。十一世紀時，波斯學者阿爾比魯尼就描述過印度教徒在新月之夜，於神廟和屋頂上點起油燈。燈的意義因地而異。在北印度，它們讓人想起羅摩王子：他在流放 14 年後回到阿約提亞，人們點燈迎接他。許多家庭也會打掃家裡，迎接財富女神拉克什米；錫克教徒和耆那教徒則紀念他們各自歷史中的事件。所有這些故事背後都是同一個概念：光明戰勝黑暗。

慶祝活動持續五天。家家戶戶上街採買，用彩色粉末或花瓣在地上畫出 rangoli 圖案，並點起一排排的燈。到了第四天，親友彼此拜訪，帶著禮物和一盒盒甜點，例如古拉布賈蒙（炸奶球）和賈勒比（糖漿炸麵圈）。

對印度的陶匠來說，這個節日還有另一層重要性。孟買某個社區的陶匠說，他們一年大約一半的營收來自排燈節前的那一個月。2016 年，一盞手工陶燈賣大約 50 美分，從國外來的塑膠燈比較便宜，只要大約 25 美分；但賣家說，想要真東西的人還是會一再回來找他們。

這個節日的規模持續擴大。2025 年 10 月 19 日，阿約提亞沿著河岸點亮了 2,617,215 盞陶燈，創下世界紀錄。煙火也很受歡迎，不過煙霧會加重空氣污染，新德里近年已經禁止施放。2025 年 12 月，排燈節被列入聯合國教科文組織的人類非物質文化遺產名錄——如今這個節日由超過十億人共享。

open_tasks.prompt: The passage says that fireworks add to air pollution during Diwali, while clay lamps are an old part of the festival. Suggest one way a city could keep the festival bright but cleaner, and explain why it could work in one or two English sentences.
reference_answers: A city could hold one shared light show by the river instead of letting every family set off fireworks, because one show makes far less smoke but still brings people together.
Families could light more clay lamps and fewer fireworks, since lamps keep the meaning of the festival and also help local potters earn money.
